analysis.one_liner: Bars Donald Trump from ever holding federal office under the Constitution's insurrection clause.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Rep. Cicilline with 41 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill declares that, under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment — which disqualifies officials who have engaged in insurrection — Donald Trump cannot again hold the presidency or any federal office. Its findings lay out hundreds of pages of evidence from the January 6 Committee, including testimony from former Trump administration officials about efforts to overturn the 2020 election. It also preserves any existing state or federal processes for enforcing the same constitutional provision.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, voters and election officials would gain a congressional finding that a president who incited an attack on the certification of an election is constitutionally barred from office again — a check on officeholders who attempt to overturn elections.

how_it_helps.text: Declares Trump ineligible under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment to hold the presidency or any federal office, civil or military [S2] [S3].
Leaves intact all existing state and federal legal processes for enforcing Section 3, so the congressional declaration would not crowd out court or state action [S3].

Its findings formally compile testimony from former Trump administration lawyers and aides — including Bill Barr, Marc Short, Greg Jacob, and Cassidy Hutchinson — documenting efforts to overturn the 2020 election and the January 6 attack [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Donald Trump personally, who would be barred from federal office, and voters who supported him, whose choice for president would be set aside by a congressional determination.

drawbacks.text: The Senate vote cited in the bill's own findings — 57 to 43 to convict Trump of incitement of insurrection in his February 2021 impeachment trial — fell short of the two-thirds majority the Constitution requires for conviction, which opponents cite as the final judgment that he was not disqualified [S3].

A statute naming a single individual and barring him from office invites the objection that Congress is legislating a penalty against one person rather than enforcing a constitutional rule generally — a serious structural concern that supporters would have had to defend in court.
The bill was symbolic in practice: with 42 supporters out of 435 House members, no Republican backing, and only two weeks left in the Congress, it had no realistic path to becoming law [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine constitutional question — whether a president who engaged in insurrection can hold office again — and its evidentiary findings are drawn directly from sworn testimony. But it was drafted as a declaration against one named individual with no enforcement machinery of its own, and it arrived with no possibility of passage, so its practical effect even if passed would have been limited to whatever weight a congressional declaration carries in later court cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the Congress, sent to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on December 15, 2022, with 41 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — its only action in the entire Congress [S5].

The bill invokes Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, the post-Civil War provision barring officials who 'engaged in insurrection or rebellion' from holding office, and Section 5, which gives Congress power to enforce the amendment by legislation [S2] [S3].
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Donald Trump came out ahead: his eligibility to run for and hold federal office was left untouched, and no member of either party ever had to vote on the disqualification question. The House leadership and committee leaders who let the bill sit also avoided a politically charged floor fight in the closing days of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Donald Trump and his eligibility to run

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill declaring Trump ineligible under the Fourteenth Amendment's insurrection clause.

for.name: 42 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in committee with no hearing or markup scheduled for the seventeen days remaining in the Congress; it received no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican backed the bill; because it never reached the floor, there was no roll-call vote to measure the split beyond party lines.

industries.industry: Donald Trump (the bill's sole named subject)
industries.note: The bill would bar this one individual from ever holding federal office, based on the finding that he engaged in insurrection. His interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the bill's stated public purpose of enforcing the constitutional disqualification.
